body.text: Historic House of Commons Gathering Demands Diplomatic Intervention

body.caption: British MPs & UKPNP Delegates Gathered at International Conference on Jammu and Kashmir.

body.text: The United Kashmir People's National Party (UKPNP) convened its 5th International Conference on Jammu and Kashmir at the House of Commons under the title 'The Jammu Kashmir Conflict and the Role of the British Government.' In a landmark gathering that filled the conference Room of Portcullis House, the conference passed 20 resolutions and issued a direct appeal to the British Government to honour its own historical principles including a little-known warning from 1848 and take a leading role in resolving the oldest unresolved conflict on the United Nations agenda.

body.caption: Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri addressing the conference.

body.text: The event was hosted by Richard Burgon, Labour Member of Parliament for Leeds East. The Chief Guest was Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri, Chairman of UKPNP. The conference was presided over by Sardar Tariq Khan, President of UKPNP United Kingdom, and moderated by Raja Sarfraz, General Secretary of UKPNP United Kingdom.

Keynote Speech Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri: Britain's Colonial Role and the 1848 Warning

body.caption: Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri & UKPNP Activists Group Photo in British Parliament.

body.text: In his keynote address, Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri delivered a detailed historical indictment of British colonial policies that shaped the tragedy of Jammu and Kashmir. He reminded the audience that the partition of the Indian subcontinent in 1947 was 'a hurried and deeply flawed process' whose consequences continue to haunt generations. He specifically named Lord Mountbatten, arguing that the last Viceroy exercised 'considerable influence upon Maharajah Hari Singh regarding the future of Jammu and Kashmir' an influence that prevented a free and independent decision.

body.caption: Conference audience listening to keynote speeches.

body.text: Kashmiri also pointed to the roles of George Cunningham and Major William Brown, whose actions during the Gilgit rebellion remain 'one of the most controversial chapters of Kashmir's history.' He stated that the Gilgit events carried immense geopolitical implications and 'undermined possibilities for an independent political course.' The people of Jammu and Kashmir, he emphasised, 'were never genuinely consulted. Their consent was absent. Their aspirations were ignored.'

The British Government declared that it would not support or protect a ruler who oppressed his people, and that if misrule continued, Britain reserved the right to intervene directly in the administration of the state.  Henry Hardinge, 1st Viscount Hardinge, 7 January 1848

body.caption: Delegates reviewing historical documents and resolutions.

body.text: Most strikingly, Kashmiri invoked a formal warning issued on 7 January 1848 by Henry Hardinge, 1st Viscount Hardinge, to Maharaja Gulab Singh shortly after the creation of the princely state under the Treaty of Amritsar (1846). He quoted the warning verbatim: 'The British Government declared that it would not support or protect a ruler who oppressed his people, and that if misrule continued, Britain reserved the right to intervene directly in the administration of the state.' Hardinge had further stated that continued oppression 'could lead to direct interference by the British, thereby reducing the ruler's independence.'

Kashmiri argued that this historical principle that governance must be accountable to the welfare of the people and that external powers cannot ignore oppression remains binding on today's British Government. 'These historical legacies require serious reflection and responsible engagement from today's British Government and leadership not to revisit the past with bitterness, but to help correct its consequences and contribute toward a peaceful and just future,' he said.
Role of the British Government: From Historical Responsibility to Present Action

body.caption: British MPs , UKPNP Leadership & Members during resolution discussions.

body.text: The conference unanimously called on the British Government to move beyond symbolism and take concrete steps. Resolution 17 explicitly urges 'the British Government to play its role in achieving a peaceful and long-lasting solution to the Jammu and Kashmir issue' and demands 'monitoring of human rights across all regions of Jammu and Kashmir, including Jammu, Kashmir, Ladakh, Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir.'

body.caption: Panellist exchanging views on human rights monitoring issues.

body.text: In his speech, Chairman Kashmiri laid out a clear set of demands: 'We are asking Britain to stand on the side of principles. To stand for democracy. To stand for the right to free movement of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. To stand for human rights. To stand for dialogue. To stand for peace. To stand for the right to self-determination of the people of Jammu and Kashmir.' He urged Britain to use its diplomatic influence and international standing 'to encourage a peaceful political process that places the people of Jammu and Kashmir at the centre of discussions regarding their future.'

The conference also noted that the European Parliament's 2007 report on Kashmir and Pakistan's constitutional Article 257 (which recognises Jammu and Kashmir as a disputed territory) further underline the unresolved status of the region. Resolution 19 requests British MPs and Members of the House of Lords to 'ensure follow-up discussions and conferences on the Jammu and Kashmir conflict.'
Call to Pakistan and Local Authorities: Restrain Force, Honour Promises to Awami Action Committees

body.caption: Delegates & UKPNP Members during Conference in British Parliament.

body.text: Drawing directly from Resolution 4, the conference issued a strong appeal to the Government of Pakistan and local authorities in Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan. The resolution urges them to 'restrain the use of force and provide basic facilities and fundamental rights to the people, while fulfilling the promises made with the Joint Awami Action Committees.' The conference further called on the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) to 'continue negotiations and dialogue with the authorities to secure their rights' and to 'remain vigilant and peaceful, because peaceful struggle, negotiations and dialogue are the only way forward.' The underlying principle, repeated by several speakers, was that no Kashmiri should be harmed in the pursuit of political demands.
Speech of Host MP Richard Burgon

body.caption: Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri , Richard Burgon MP, Iqbal Mohammad MP & Panellist of the Conference.

body.text: Host MP Richard Burgon reaffirmed that the British Parliament has 'both a historical responsibility and a contemporary moral duty' to address the Kashmir question with seriousness and impartiality. He pledged continued parliamentary support for initiatives that amplify Kashmiri voices and explicitly backed the right of the Kashmiri people to self-determination.

Burgon stated: 'I am delighted to welcome all of you here today in such large numbers for the 5th International Conference on Jammu and Kashmir, organised by the United Kashmir People's National Party here in the British Parliament. I warmly welcome Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri, the leadership of UKPNP, distinguished guests, Members of Parliament, members of civil society, journalists, youth representatives, and all participants who have travelled from across the United Kingdom to attend this important conference. I am pleased to continue engaging and working with UKPNP, a secular political organisation that believes in democracy, the rule of law, equality, dignity, peaceful political struggle, and fundamental human rights for all people without discrimination.'

'I am especially encouraged to see such a large number of young Kashmiris participating today. Their presence demonstrates that the values of peace, democracy, justice, and self-determination are gaining greater support with every passing day. This is an important achievement and a strong source of encouragement for all of us. There are several important meetings, discussions, and engagements taking place across Parliament at this time, and I am grateful to fellow Members of Parliament who have taken time from their busy schedules to join us today. We have invited and are expecting additional MPs and parliamentary colleagues who will share their insights, experiences, and perspectives during this conference. Their participation reflects the growing interest and concern within Parliament regarding the situation in Jammu and Kashmir.'

'For many years, we have continued to raise the issue of Jammu and Kashmir in Parliament and to highlight the difficulties, suffering, and human rights concerns faced by the people across all regions of Jammu and Kashmir. The Jammu and Kashmir issue is not merely a bilateral or territorial dispute between India and Pakistan. It remains an international issue that has been on the United Nations agenda since 1948. We support the right of the people of Jammu and Kashmir to self-determination. The people of Jammu and Kashmir must have the democratic right to decide their own future freely and fairly. They must also enjoy freedom of movement, freedom of expression, political participation, and all fundamental human rights guaranteed under international law.'

'We must continue to support peaceful dialogue, democratic engagement, and non-violent political processes as the only path toward a just and lasting peace. Violence, extremism, hatred, and the suppression of freedoms can never provide a sustainable solution. We are also deeply concerned by restrictions on civil liberties, arbitrary detentions, suppression of political voices, demographic changes, and the continuing suffering of divided families across the region. The voices of ordinary Kashmiris must be heard, respected, and protected. This conference is an opportunity to strengthen dialogue, raise awareness, and encourage constructive international engagement for peace, justice, accountability, and human dignity. I thank all speakers, organisers, and participants for being here today and for continuing to raise awareness of one of the longest unresolved issues on the international agenda,' he concluded.
Special Message from MP Fabian Hamilton

body.caption: UKPNP Activists Huge Gathering in the Front of British Parliament.

body.text: MP Fabian Hamilton sent a special message expressing solidarity with the Kashmiri people and reaffirming his support for a united, secular, and democratic Jammu and Kashmir where people can determine their own future freely.

'Fabian Hamilton MP addressed the conference through a special message and apologised for not being able to attend the meeting in person. He warmly greeted the participants and expressed his hope that the conference discussions were progressing successfully. The Labour MP stated that the issue of Jammu and Kashmir remains very close to the hearts of many Members of Parliament, including himself. He said he hoped that the Kashmiri community in the United Kingdom, especially in Leeds and across West Yorkshire, recognised that many British parliamentarians genuinely care about the people of Kashmir and the families who continue to live in the region.'

'Fabian Hamilton reaffirmed his support for a united, secular, and democratic Jammu and Kashmir where people are able to determine their own future freely and peacefully. He stressed that the people of Kashmir should not be forced to accept decisions imposed upon them by any external power. He explained that this commitment to justice and self-determination is the reason why Richard Burgon MP, himself, and many other parliamentarians continue to raise the issue of Kashmir and support the rights of the Kashmiri people. The MP stated that Kashmir remains an unresolved issue that requires a fair and peaceful solution based on justice, democracy, and the right to self-determination. He pledged that British parliamentarians supporting the Kashmiri cause would continue offering their solidarity and support for as long as necessary. Fabian Hamilton concluded by expressing hope that a just resolution would eventually be achieved, one that respects the rights, dignity, and aspirations of all the men, women, and children of Jammu and Kashmir. He thanked the organisers and participants of the conference and encouraged them to continue discussing constructive ways forward for peace, justice, and democratic engagement regarding the Kashmir issue.'
Speech of MP Tahir Ali

body.caption: Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri addressing the conference.

body.text: MP Tahir Ali reaffirmed support for Kashmiri self-determination and criticised the human rights situation in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, particularly the revocation of Articles 370 and 35A.

Tahir Ali MP began by thanking the Chair for giving him the opportunity to speak. He said he had not expected to walk into the meeting and immediately be asked to say a few words, but he was pleased to join the conference and stand with those who continue to raise the issue of Jammu and Kashmir. He thanked Richard Burgon MP for hosting the conference in the British Parliament and welcomed Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri, Chairman of the United Kashmir People's National Party (UKPNP), in the UK Parliament. He thanked UKPNP for bringing this important discussion to Westminster. He acknowledged that the struggle of the Kashmiri people has continued for many decades, particularly since October 1947, and said it remains one of the longest unresolved political issues in the world.

Tahir Ali MP made it clear that Kashmir should not be treated simply as a dispute between India and Pakistan. He stressed that the issue of Jammu and Kashmir is an international matter and that the international community has a responsibility to address it. Referring to the historical background, he noted that the matter was taken to the United Nations in January 1948. He said this history proves that Kashmir has never been only a bilateral matter, but an issue connected to international law, peace, justice, and the right of people to determine their own future. He also reminded the audience that the partition of the subcontinent took place under a British Labour Government. For that reason, he argued, Britain carries a special responsibility toward the Kashmiri people. He said the Kashmiri people are not asking for anything extraordinary. They are asking for their basic and recognised right to self-determination.

Tahir Ali MP expressed concern that more than 70 years have passed, yet the people of Jammu and Kashmir are still waiting for justice. He said such a long delay is unacceptable and has caused deep pain for Kashmiris in the region and for the Kashmiri diaspora across the world. He strongly criticised the human rights situation in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir. He referred to the atrocities being reported there and highlighted the revocation of Articles 370 and 35A in 2019 as a turning point that further damaged the rights and autonomy of the Kashmiri people. He said the silence of the international community is deeply disappointing. However, he assured the audience that the Kashmiri people are not alone. He stated that voices inside the British Parliament will continue to raise this issue and will not allow it to disappear from the political agenda. Tahir Ali MP said that wherever Kashmiris live, including here in the United Kingdom, their voice must be heard. He pledged that he and others in Parliament would continue to speak for justice, human rights, and the right to self-determination. He concluded by reaffirming his solidarity with the Kashmiri people and said that the flag of justice for Kashmir will continue to be raised until the people of Jammu and Kashmir are allowed to decide their own future freely and democratically.
Speech of MP Imran Hussain

body.caption: Participants  at the UKPNP 5th International Conference on Jammu Kashmir in House of Commons.

body.text: Imran Hussain MP began by warmly welcoming everyone present at the conference and acknowledged the many people who had travelled from across the country to attend such an important gathering. He apologised for arriving late, explaining that Parliament often has several commitments taking place simultaneously. He expressed confidence that the meeting was already in very good hands with his friend, colleague, and fellow Labour MP Richard Burgon.

Speaking about Richard Burgon, Imran Hussain described him as a true friend of the Kashmiri people and someone with whom he works very closely, particularly on issues of international injustice. In a light-hearted moment, he joked that the two are often described as 'twins,' adding humorously that he was not sure who that was worse for. He stressed, however, that both of them remain committed to speaking out wherever injustice occurs in the world.

He thanked and congratulated UKPNP for organising this very impressive and well attended conference. Imran Hussain highlighted the growth of the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Kashmir over recent years. Since taking on the role of Chair, he said he had approached the position with a serious vision and determination to strengthen parliamentary engagement on Kashmir. He expressed pride that the APPG has continued to grow and now brings together MPs from several political parties who are committed to supporting the issue of Kashmir.

He underlined the importance of grassroots support and praised Kashmiri communities and campaigners across the United Kingdom who continue to challenge injustice and raise awareness. According to him, momentum is steadily growing across the country, with more people becoming engaged and involved in the movement.

Imran Hussain emphasised that all Kashmiri groups and organisations must work together. He encouraged unity among grassroots organisations and stressed that, at the heart of the struggle, everyone is united by one central principle: the right of the Kashmiri people to self-determination. He stated clearly that the future of Kashmir should not be decided by others, but by the Kashmiri people themselves.

The Labour MP also expressed his delight at seeing many young people attending the conference. He stressed the need to involve younger generations more actively in grassroots activism and campaigning, explaining that stronger public engagement would encourage more Members of Parliament to take up the issue. MPs, he noted, listen to their constituents, and therefore Kashmiri communities must continue presenting their case effectively in every constituency possible.

Imran Hussain said he wants the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Kashmir to become stronger and louder, because only sustained pressure and advocacy can force governments to listen seriously to the issue.

Turning to the situation in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, he stated that the persecution of Kashmiris is widely known and has significantly intensified since the revocation of Articles 370 and 35A in August 2019. He argued that the policies pursued by the Indian government were aimed at suppressing the Kashmiri struggle for self-determination.

He referred to increasing human rights abuses, arbitrary arrests, and the growing number of political prisoners in the region. Despite these developments, he declared that every attempt to suppress the movement for self-determination would only strengthen the resolve of those speaking out against injustice.

Imran Hussain thanked all participants for their continued commitment and activism. He stressed that meetings such as this, combined with grassroots mobilisation and political engagement, can make a real difference. He strongly rejected the argument repeatedly advanced by successive governments that Kashmir is merely a bilateral issue between India and Pakistan. Reaffirming his position, he declared that Kashmir is an unresolved international issue that requires international attention and resolution.

He pledged that the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Kashmir would continue pressing the British Government to recognise this reality and to take meaningful steps toward justice, accountability, and the protection of fundamental rights for the people of Jammu and Kashmir.

The MP further connected the Kashmir issue to wider global crises and the weakening of the international rules-based order. He referenced the continuing war and humanitarian crisis in Gaza, the persecution of the Rohingya people, and other international conflicts as examples of failures to uphold international law and justice. He argued that the Kashmir conflict cannot continue to be ignored if peace, stability, and prosperity are to be achieved in South Asia. Referring to India and Pakistan as two nuclear powers, he stressed that Kashmir remains the central unresolved issue between them and therefore must be brought to the forefront of the international agenda. Concluding his address, Imran Hussain said that the large turnout at the conference demonstrated the strong and continuing support for the Kashmiri cause. He thanked attendees, including members of his own constituency who had travelled to participate, and expressed his gratitude to everyone involved in organising and supporting the event. He ended by reaffirming his commitment to continue raising the voice of the Kashmiri people in Parliament and beyond.
The 20 Resolutions: Free Movement, Expression, Self-Determination and a United Secular State
The conference unanimously passed 20 detailed resolutions. Among the most significant:
• Resolution 1 commits to a peaceful, democratic struggle, rejecting violence, terrorism and religious extremism.
• Resolution 2 declares the conflict a human tragedy, not a mere bilateral territorial dispute.
• Resolution 3 demands transparent investigation of crimes against humanity.

• Resolution 4 calls on Pakistan and local authorities to restrain force and fulfil promises to Awami Action Committees, and urges the committees to remain peaceful. Called on the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) to 'continue negotiations and dialogue with the authorities to secure their rights' and to 'remain vigilant and peaceful, because peaceful struggle, negotiations and dialogue are the only way forward.'
• Resolution 5 demands fair proportional representation for Jammu and Kashmir refugees in the Azad Kashmir Legislative Assembly and cancellation of fake domicile certificates.
• Resolution 6 supports the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly's demand to restore special status and full statehood of Jammu and Kashmir.

• Resolution 7 demands the immediate and unconditional release of all peaceful political activists and human rights defenders, and strongly opposes restrictions on freedom of expression, assembly, speech, and free movement.
• Resolution 8 calls for repeal of repressive laws that exclude pro-Kashmir parties, including UKPNP, from elections.
• Resolution 9 demands justice for the extrajudicial killing of brothers Zarnosh and Jibran Nasim in Rawalakot.
• Resolution 10 condemns the abduction of children (Saad Haroon, 8; Arslan Zubair, 2; Muhammad Tabish Khan, 3) and police harassment of their families.
• Resolution 11 warns against demographic changes violating the 1927 State Subject Rule.

• Resolution 15 declares that freedom of movement is a fundamental right and demands that all State Subject Certificate holders be allowed to travel freely across all regions of the State of Jammu and Kashmir. It also calls for reopening historic trade and travel routes to reunite divided families.

• Resolution 16 reaffirms the right to self-determination of the Kashmiri people, as enshrined in Article 1 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, stressing that 'their political future must be determined freely and without coercion.'
• Resolution 17 urges the British Government to monitor human rights across all parts of the divided state.
• Resolution 18 appreciates peace dialogues (e.g. US-Iran in Pakistan) and calls for peaceful resolution of all international conflicts.
• Resolution 19 requests continued engagement of the British Parliament.
• Resolution 20 declares a continued struggle for 'a united, secular and independent State of Jammu and Kashmir for all people.'
Closing Declaration: Justice, Not Sympathy

Sardar Tariq Khan, presiding over the conference, underlined the unity of the Kashmiri diaspora and their commitment to lawful, persistent advocacy. Raja Sarfraz noted that the strong presence of women and youth signalled a generational shift in the movement.

Chairman Sardar Shaukat Ali Kashmiri closed with these words: 'The people of Jammu and Kashmir do not seek sympathy. They seek recognition of their humanity. History ultimately judges’ nations and leaders not by the power they possess, but by the justice they uphold. Let us work together for a future where South Asia becomes a region of peace rather than confrontation; cooperation rather than hostility; and hope rather than despair.'
About UKPNP

The United Kashmir People's National Party (UKPNP) is a leading secular, democratic representative organisation of the people of Jammu Kashmir and Kashmiri diaspora. UKPNP strongly opposes violence, extremism, religious hatred, racial discrimination, advocating peacefully for the political and human rights of the Kashmiri people through democratic and parliamentary channels across the United Kingdom, United Nations, Europe, the United States and across the globe.
